title: How I Prove to My Students that They Actually Can Memorize Things
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. argues that memorization still matters in the age of Google because knowing things facilitates further knowledge-building, critical thinking and literacy. He walks through a fifteen-minute activity from his history classes in which students memorize a short list of five must-know dates through repeated cycles of writing from memory, correcting against the original, and re-attempting. The activity is bracketed by quickwrites asking whether students are the kind of people who can memorize, so the experience itself becomes evidence against a fixed self-image. He explains that the lesson serves both his year-long knowledge-building campaign and his key beliefs of credibility, value, effort, success and identity. His final caution is that memorized knowledge must be meaningful and revisited in later lessons or it will not stick.
points: Memorization is defended as one legitimate route to knowledge, which in turn supports critical thinking and literacy, rather than something Google has made obsolete.
The activity uses a five-item list and four write-from-memory cycles with self-scoring, so nearly every student visibly improves from List 2 to List 3.
Opening and closing quickwrites about whether I am a person who can memorize turn the exercise into evidence that challenges students' fixed beliefs about themselves.
Starting small and explicitly guiding the process lets students succeed quickly, which builds the belief that effort pays off.
Memorized facts only stick when they are meaningful and revisited in later readings, writings and discussions; one-off memorization is wasted.
quotes: Knowing things — rather than being able to Google things — facilitates further knowledge-building, critical thinking, and literacy. There are many ways we can come to know things — incidental learning, topic immersion, inquiry, and so on — and one of those ways is just straight-up memorization.

Near the start of the school year before I give my kids their first list like this, I have them write a 100-word quickwrite warm-up on the following prompt: Are you the kind of person who can memorize a list of dates? How do you know? What kinds of things in your life do you memorize, and how do you do that?

Step Two: Cover up your list, and now write that list of dates from memory. (I black out the projector at this point.) Write down every scrap that you can remember — every bit of numbers, every bit of event description. It's okay to be wrong — get as much down as you can. (I give 1-2 minutes here.)
And then, I want you to make List 2 perfect, just like List 1. Cross things out, erase, use arrows, but make List 2 perfect.

Step Five: Okay. Get out Lists 1 and 2 and use them to correct List 3. Again, give yourself a score, and again, make List 3 perfect, like Lists 1 and 2. How many people improved their score from List 2 to List 3? (At this point, almost all hands go up.)
Memorization isn't our “thing” — long-term flourishing is — but it's one activity we'll come back to repeatedly to strengthen our minds and hearts throughout the year.
It doesn't matter that there's Google — I want it in their brains, and I want to show them that there's a lot of under-advertised joy in this old-fashioned idea of building knowledge.
